meta_desc: Probate is the Surrogate's Court process that validates a will and empowers the executor. How it works in New York, what skips it, and how long it takes.
direct_answer: Probate is the court process that makes a will official. In New York, the Surrogate's Court in the county where the person lived reviews the will, confirms it was validly signed, and appoints the executor by issuing letters testamentary. Only then does the executor have legal authority to collect the assets, pay the debts, and distribute what remains to the beneficiaries. If there is no will, a similar proceeding called administration appoints an administrator instead.

sections.h2: How Probate Works In New York, Step By Step
sections.html:
Probate follows a fairly predictable sequence:

  • Filing. The nominated executor files a petition with the Surrogate's Court, along with the original will and a certified death certificate.
  • Notice. The closest relatives — the people who would inherit if there were no will — must be formally notified. They either sign waivers consenting to probate or are served with a citation, which gives them a chance to raise objections.
  • Review. The court examines the will for proper signing and witnessing. If no one objects and the paperwork is in order, the will is admitted to probate.
  • Letters testamentary. The court issues the executor official proof of authority, which banks, brokerages, and title companies require.
  • Administration of the estate. The executor gathers assets, pays valid debts and taxes, and then distributes the balance under the will.
  • Closing. Beneficiaries sign receipts and releases, or the executor files an accounting for court approval.

Two terms are worth translating. Letters testamentary are simply the court's certificate of the executor's authority — the document banks and buyers ask to see. Admitting the will means the court has accepted it as the deceased person's valid final word; from that point, its instructions control the estate.

sections.h2: What Property Goes Through Probate — And What Skips It
sections.html:
Probate only reaches assets that were titled in the deceased person's sole name with no built-in transfer mechanism. A surprising amount of wealth passes outside the process entirely:

  • Jointly owned property with rights of survivorship goes automatically to the surviving owner.
  • Life insurance and retirement accounts go directly to the named beneficiaries.
  • Bank accounts with payable-on-death or in-trust-for designations transfer on presentation of a death certificate.
  • Assets held in a living trust are distributed by the trustee under the trust's terms.

New York also offers a shortcut for modest estates: when the personal property left behind is worth $50,000 or less, a simplified proceeding called voluntary administration can substitute for full probate. It does not cover real estate.

sections.h2: How Long Probate Takes And What Shapes The Timeline
sections.html:
For an uncontested estate with cooperative family members, getting a will admitted and letters issued often takes weeks to a few months, depending on the county's volume and the completeness of the paperwork. The full administration takes longer. Creditors generally have seven months from the executor's appointment to present claims, so careful executors rarely make final distributions before that window closes. Add time for selling a house, filing final tax returns, or resolving disputes, and a typical estate wraps up in roughly a year — faster for simple ones.

Contested matters are a different world. Objections to a will, fights over the choice of fiduciary, or accounting disputes convert probate into litigation, which is measured in years, not months. That risk is why families are often counseled to keep relatives informed early — probate runs smoothest when no one is surprised.

If you are the nominated executor, the best early moves are simple: locate the original will, order several certified death certificates, and secure the property. If you are a family member waiting on the process, know that quiet stretches are usually procedure at work, not misconduct.

takeaways: Probate is Surrogate's Court review that validates the will and gives the executor legal authority.
Without a will, the parallel process is called administration and intestacy rules decide who inherits.
Joint accounts, beneficiary designations, and trust assets pass outside probate.
Small estates with $50,000 or less in personal property may qualify for simplified voluntary administration.
Uncontested probate often takes months; the seven-month creditor period shapes distribution timing; contests take years.
faq_short: Probate is the New York Surrogate's Court process of proving a will is valid and appointing the executor through letters testamentary. The executor then collects assets, pays debts and taxes, and distributes the remainder under the will. Assets with joint owners, named beneficiaries, or trust ownership skip probate, and estates with $50,000 or less in personal property may use a simplified proceeding.
